title: Split Array into Consecutive Subsequences
description: Brute force to optimized: greedy extension with two hash maps tracking remaining counts and subsequence ends.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums sorted in non decreasing order, determine whether it can be split into one or more subsequences, where each subsequence consists of consecutive integers and has a length of at least 3.

blocks.caption: Greedily extend an existing run whenever possible, otherwise start a fresh run of 3

blocks.title: Analogy: Dealing a Sorted Hand of Cards Into Valid Straights
blocks.text: Like dealing a sorted hand of numbered cards into separate straights, where every straight must contain at least 3 consecutive numbers, deciding for each card whether it extends an existing straight or starts a brand new one.

blocks.caption: Split the sorted array into groups of consecutive numbers, each group at least length 3

blocks.text: No valid split exists here that gives every group a length of at least 3 (one attempted split leaves a leftover group of length 2), so the answer is false.

Before writing any code, notice that scanning nums in order and deciding, for each number, "does this extend something already started, or do I need to start something new" is a natural greedy structure, and greedy structures need a reason why the greedy choice can never backfire.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since nums is sorted, when a number is reached, every subsequence that could ever be extended by it must already exist and must end exactly one less than it, so checking "does anything currently end at value minus 1" is the complete extension check.

Observation 2: If nothing can be extended, the only other option is starting a brand new subsequence, which requires this value and the next two consecutive values to still be available.

Observation 3: Between these two options, extending an existing subsequence is always at least as good as starting a new one: a subsequence that is already valid, length 3 or more, only gets more flexible by growing longer, since a longer valid group is still valid, while a number not used to extend might be needed later to complete some other group's minimum length of 3.

Observation 4: Because this preference is always safe, the decision at every number becomes purely mechanical: check one hash map for an extendable ending, and if that fails, check another hash map of remaining counts for the two following values, no backtracking or reconsideration ever needed.

Whenever a greedy choice can be shown to never make later choices worse, an exchange argument where swapping a "new start" for an "extension" never hurts, commit to it fully and implement it with direct O(1) lookups instead of any search or backtracking.

The real subtlety in this problem is not speeding anything up further, both approaches already run in O(n), it is correctly justifying why greedily preferring extension over starting fresh is always safe, and then implementing that justified rule cleanly with exactly two hash maps.

Maintain counts of how many times each value still needs to be placed, and for each value in order, scan for an existing valid subsequence it could be appended to by checking, from scratch, how many subsequences currently end at the value just before it.

items: Count the remaining occurrences of every value.
For each number, scan to see whether a subsequence ending at the previous value can be extended.
If not, check whether a brand new subsequence of length 3 can be started using this value and the next two.
If neither is possible, the array cannot be split validly.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Skipping when a value's remaining count is 0 avoids reconsidering any value that has already been fully consumed by earlier decisions, since every occurrence of a number is placed into exactly one subsequence, never reused.

The extension check is written as a loop over a single-element list, functionally identical to a direct if check, but structured this way to make the extension attempt read as one explicit, isolated step before falling through to the new-subsequence attempt.

The new-subsequence check tests availability of both the next value and the one after it together, since starting a valid length-3 run needs both of the next two consecutive values to still be available, not just one.

blocks.text: Every number is either appended to an existing valid subsequence or used to start a fresh length 3 subsequence, correctly greedy since always preferring to extend an existing subsequence never hurts, a longer subsequence is still valid.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass, since each map lookup is O(1) on average.
Space: O(n), for the count and ends maps.

Limitation: this greedy approach is actually already close to optimal in complexity, the real refinement is stating precisely why the "always prefer extending" greedy rule is provably correct rather than just applying it.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Unusually for a "brute force to optimized" progression, both versions here already run in O(n) time using the exact same two hash maps, since the correct greedy rule was already being applied. What actually changes is not complexity but clarity and confidence: the earlier version wraps the extension check inside a single-element loop and an "appended" flag, structure that obscures the fact that this is really just one direct condition. Stripping that down to a plain if, else-if, else directly mirrors the three logical outcomes for any number: extend, start fresh, or fail, making the greedy exchange argument, and the code implementing it, easy to state and verify together. This is a case where "optimizing" means simplifying the implementation to directly match the proven-correct logic, not reducing asymptotic cost, since there was no further cost left to remove.

The greedy rule works because ending a subsequence exactly where it is never creates a problem: any subsequence of length 3 or more is already valid, and choosing to extend it further only ever helps place more numbers, never hurts. Formalizing this into the two hash maps, remaining counts, and subsequences currently ending at each value, makes every decision an O(1) lookup, which is exactly what the approach above already does. The remaining optimization is purely about implementation clarity: using two clean maps built once, rather than any redundant rescanning.
The same two hash map approach, with clean state: remaining counts and subsequences currently ending at each value.

blocks.caption: Optimized: greedily extend an existing run ending one less, or start a fresh run of 3

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with O(1) average map operations.
Space: O(n), for the two hash maps.

ends[v] correctly tracks how many subsequences currently have v as their most recent, largest, element, so checking ends at num minus 1 answers exactly the right question: does some subsequence exist that this specific number would extend? Because the greedy preference for extension over starting fresh is provably safe, an already-valid subsequence only becomes more flexible by growing, never less, always taking the extension path when available, and only falling back to starting fresh when it is not, is guaranteed to find a valid split whenever one exists.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation for the current number","Action taken"],"rows":[["A subsequence already ends at num minus 1","Extend it: move the ending marker from num minus 1 to num"],["No subsequence ends at num minus 1, but num plus 1 and num plus 2 are both still available","Start a brand new subsequence using num, num plus 1, and num plus 2"],["Neither option is possible","No valid split exists; return false immediately"]]}

items: count is built once, in a single pass, before any placement decisions begin, so every lookup against it reflects the true remaining supply of each value at that point in the scan.

Skipping a number whose remaining count is already 0 handles duplicate values correctly, since a number that has already been fully placed by an earlier decision should not trigger a second, redundant decision.

The extension branch decrements the count of subsequences ending at num minus 1 and increments the count ending at num together, correctly modeling that the same subsequence has simply grown by one, not that a new one was created.
The new-subsequence branch consumes the next two values from count immediately, ensuring they cannot be mistakenly reused as the start of some other subsequence later in the scan.

blocks.text: The greedy "always prefer extending an existing subsequence over starting a new one" rule is provably safe here because a longer valid subsequence never becomes a problem later, only ever helps, which is the exchange argument that justifies the greedy choice.

items: Preferring to start a new subsequence over extending an existing one, which can leave a shorter, invalid group behind that could have been avoided, since a number spent on a fresh start might have been the only thing keeping some other group above length 3.
Forgetting to decrement the remaining count for a number when it gets consumed, causing it to be considered available again later and potentially double-counted into two different subsequences.
Checking availability of only one of the next two values instead of requiring both, which could start an invalid "subsequence" that is actually missing one of its required consecutive members.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["An array shorter than 3 elements","Can never be split validly and should return false immediately, since no group of length at least 3 can ever be formed"],["An array that is one single run of consecutive numbers of length exactly 3","The minimum valid case, correctly returning true since one full group is formed with nothing left over"]]}

items: State the greedy exchange argument explicitly: extending an existing subsequence can never be worse than starting a new one, since any number that could complete a new length-3 group could equally well extend an already-valid longer group.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Greedily decide to extend an existing group or start a new one" points toward asking whether an exchange argument justifies always preferring extension, and if so, implementing the decision as two direct hash map checks, not a search or backtracking.

items: How would you prove the greedy exchange argument rigorously, not just intuitively? Assume an optimal solution starts a new subsequence with a number that could have extended an existing one instead; swapping that choice never decreases any group's length and never breaks any other group, so an equally valid solution using the greedy rule always exists.

What if the minimum required subsequence length were something other than 3? The same two-hash-map technique still applies, but the "start a new subsequence" branch must check for that many consecutive available values instead of exactly 2 more.

How would you also reconstruct and return the actual subsequences, not just whether a valid split exists? Track each subsequence's members explicitly, for example as a list keyed by its current ending value, instead of only counting how many end at each value.
Same greedy-with-exchange-argument structure as interval scheduling and other "always prefer the locally safest choice" greedy algorithms.
Same "two hash maps: what remains, and what state currently exists" bookkeeping style as Maximum Frequency Stack's frequency and group-stack maps.
Same "sorted input enables a single forward greedy pass" insight as many array problems where sorting first turns a search into a direct scan.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force and optimized converge to the same technique here: O(n) time, O(n) space, using two hash maps tracking remaining counts and subsequence ends.

items: Pattern: Greedy extension-preferred grouping into consecutive runs, backed by two hash maps
Core Idea: Always prefer extending an existing valid subsequence over starting a new one, since a longer valid group only ever helps and never hurts later placements
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n), for the remaining-count and subsequence-ending hash maps
Most Important Observation: A greedy rule is only trustworthy once an exchange argument proves it can never make a later outcome worse; here, extending over starting fresh is exactly such a safe rule
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Always extend if you can; only start fresh when you truly must
